content: Oral contraceptives are available in various formulations, primarily categorized into combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) and progestogen-only pills (POPs). COCPs contain both estrogen and synthetic progestogens (referred to as progestins in the United States), while POPs contain only progestogen. Combined oral contraceptive pills are further classified based on the estrogen dose and whether the doses of estrogen or progestogen remain constant or vary throughout the cycle. These pills typically function by inhibiting ovulation, thickening cervical mucus to prevent sperm penetration, and thinning the endometrial lining, which may theoretically interfere with blastocyst implantation. COCPs universally include an estrogen component, either ethinyl estradiol or mestranol. Mestranol, the inactive 3-methyl ether of ethinyl estradiol, requires hepatic metabolism to convert into active ethinyl estradiol. Fifty micrograms of mestranol is equivalent to 35 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol. Mestranol was the estrogen used in the first oral contraceptive, Enovid, but is not suitable for high-dose estrogen requirements (e.g., 50 µg ethinyl estradiol). COCPs are generally taken for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day gap during which withdrawal bleeding occurs. This bleeding is often mischaracterized as a menstrual period. These pills vary in estrogen content and are classified as monophasic (constant doses of estrogen and progestogen throughout the 21 days) or multiphasic (varying doses). Some newer formulations, such as Seasonale, have demonstrated the ability to reduce the frequency of menstrual intervals. Monophasic Pills Monophasic pills typically consist of 21 active tablets containing both estrogen and progestogen, followed by 7 placebo or iron supplement tablets. Some newer formulations include more active tablets and fewer placebos. Everyday regimens, such as Microgynon 30 ED, Femodene ED, and Logynon ED, include seven inactive placebo pills but are infrequently used in UK practice. Examples of monophasic formulations include: 1000 µg norethindrone (e.g., Norimin in the UK, Ortho-Novum 1/35 in the US) 1000 µg ethynodiol diacetate (e.g., Demulen 1/35 in the US) 250 µg norgestimate (e.g., Cilest in the UK, Ortho Cyclen in the US) 2000 µg cyproterone acetate (e.g., Dianette in the UK, used for severe acne or hirsutism) 50 µg mestranol (equivalent to 35 µg ethinyl estradiol) with 1000 µg norethindrone (e.g., Norinyl-1 in the UK, Ortho-Novum 1/50 in the US) Multiphasic Pills Multiphasic pills are designed to mimic the natural hormonal fluctuations of the menstrual cycle by varying the doses of estrogen and progestogen throughout the cycle. These include biphasic and triphasic formulations. Examples of triphasic formulations include: Ethinyl estradiol/norgestimate combinations with varying doses (e.g., Ortho Tri-Cyclen Lo in the US) Ethinyl estradiol/desogestrel combinations with varying doses (e.g., Cyclessa in the US) Ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone acetate combinations with varying doses (e.g., Estrostep Fe in the US) Ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel combinations with varying doses (e.g., Trinordiol in the UK, Triphasil in the US) Ethinyl estradiol/gestodene combinations with varying doses (e.g., Triadene in the UK) Biphasic formulations include: Ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone combinations with two distinct dose phases (e.g., Ortho-Novum 10/11 in the US, BiNovum in the UK). Progestogen-Only Pills (POPs) Progestogen-only pills contain only progestogen and are taken continuously without a break between packs. Women using POPs may experience irregular light bleeding initially, which typically stabilizes into a regular pattern over time.
